Before any page content is exchanged, the browser and server perform a handshake. MDN describes the handshake as setting the security parameters of the connection through several agreements [1].

First, the two sides agree on which version of TLS to use. MDN says the current version is TLS 1.3, defined in RFC 8446, and it is the most widely used. TLS 1.2 is still used by some websites, while TLS 1.1 and 1.0 should no longer be used [1].

Second, they agree on a cipher suite, which defines the algorithms for key agreement, authentication, encryption, and message authentication [1]. Think of the cipher suite as the toolkit both sides have chosen to use for the rest of the conversation.

Third, authentication takes place. MDN notes that the client and server can optionally authenticate each other, but on the web, client authentication is rare outside specialized applications. Server authentication, in which the server proves who it is to the client, is a fundamental part of web security [1].

Finally, they agree on a secret key used to encrypt and decrypt the messages that follow [1]. From there, the page loads as it would over plain HTTP, only protected.

The importance of server identity

Encryption alone is not enough. If you encrypted a message but sent it to an impostor, the impostor could read it. This is why server authentication matters.

MDN explains that to support it, a website needs a digital certificate containing a digitally signed copy of the public key that matches the site's private key. The certificate binds those keys to the domain name, so the browser knows it is really connecting to, for example, the intended site rather than a lookalike [1]. The signature comes from a certificate authority, or CA, an organization browsers have been configured to trust. The browser checks the signature and the domain name before it relies on the connection. The details of which authorities each browser trusts are set by the browser and operating system vendors, and are beyond the scope of the sources used here.

How a free certificate is issued

Certificates used to involve manual paperwork and fees. Let's Encrypt, which MDN describes as a widely used nonprofit certificate authority that issues free TLS certificates [1], automates the process. Its documentation says the goal of Let's Encrypt and the ACME protocol is to let a server set up HTTPS and obtain browser-trusted certificates automatically, without human intervention, by running an ACME client on the web server [2].

The process has two parts. First, the ACME client proves to the CA that the server controls a domain. The client generates an account key pair and asks the CA what it must do to prove control. According to Let's Encrypt, the CA may offer challenges such as provisioning a DNS record under the domain or placing a specific file at a well-known path on the domain's HTTP site [2]. The client completes one, and the CA checks that the challenge was satisfied.

There is a subtlety here that Let's Encrypt openly acknowledges: this validation cannot use HTTPS, which makes it vulnerable to certain attacks. To reduce the risk, the CA performs several validations in parallel from different network perspectives, making it significantly harder for an attacker to subvert the process [2].

Second, once the client is authorized for the domain, it can request a certificate. The client builds a certificate signing request asking the CA to issue a certificate for the domain with a specified public key, signed with the corresponding private key. It also signs the request with the authorized account key. The CA verifies both signatures, issues the certificate, and returns it. It also submits the certificate to public Certificate Transparency logs [2]. Renewing a certificate means repeating validation and issuance, and revocation works similarly: the client signs a request, and the CA publishes revocation information through a Certificate Revocation List so browsers know not to accept the certificate [2].

For many site owners none of this is visible. MDN observes that modern hosting services support HTTPS by default or through a setting, and the service is likely to manage the certificate and server configuration for you [1]. This is the situation for many static-site hosts, so a person publishing a blog may only need to enable an option rather than run an ACME client.

Mixed content: when one HTTP file spoils the page

A padlock for the main page does not guarantee that everything on the page is protected. MDN defines mixed content as a page loaded over HTTPS that includes scripts, stylesheets, images, or fonts over HTTP. Those subresources do not get the protection of HTTPS, so an attacker can read them and potentially modify them, which can undermine the whole page. MDN gives the example of an attacker changing a script so it behaves harmfully [1].

Because of this, browsers do not allow secure pages to load insecure subresources. Depending on the type of subresource, they either upgrade the request to HTTPS or block it [1]. A site owner who sees broken images or scripts after moving to HTTPS should look for old http:// links in the page source. If updating the code is impossible, for example for archived HTML, MDN says a content security policy with the upgrade-insecure-requests directive can make the browser upgrade those requests automatically [1].

Redirects and HSTS

People still type http://example.org or follow old links. MDN recommends that a site listen for HTTP requests and send a 301 Moved Permanently redirect to the HTTPS version. But it points out a weakness: the first request travels unprotected, so an attacker may intercept it and prevent the upgrade. This is sometimes called an SSL stripping attack [1].

The defense is the Strict-Transport-Security header, known as HSTS. It tells the browser the site wants HTTPS only, so subsequent visits go straight to HTTPS even if the user types an HTTP address. MDN notes the remaining gap: the first visit, or the first visit after the HSTS record has expired, is still exposed. To cover that, Chrome keeps an HSTS preload list of domains that are always upgraded, and Safari and Firefox use similar lists derived from Chrome's [1].

What the lock does not tell you

The sources above describe encryption, server authentication, and integrity. They do not claim that a site with a certificate is trustworthy in every other sense. A certificate links a key to a domain name, as MDN puts it [1]; it does not review the owner's honesty. A scam site can use HTTPS too, since Let's Encrypt automates issuing certificates to anyone who proves control of a domain [2]. That is an inference from how the automated process works, and not a claim either source makes in these words. Use the lock as evidence that the connection is private and goes to the domain shown, then still check that the domain is the one you meant to visit.

A short checklist for site owners

Use TLS 1.3, with 1.2 as a fallback if you must, and avoid TLS 1.0 and 1.1 [1]. Let your host or an ACME client manage certificates and renewal [1][2]. Load every script, style, image, and font over HTTPS to avoid mixed content [1]. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and add the HSTS header [1]. MDN also points to Mozilla's recommended TLS configurations and its HTTP Observatory for testing your setup [1]. Run a test after any change.

Takeaway

HTTPS combines three jobs: encrypting traffic, proving the server's identity with a certificate, and detecting tampering. The TLS handshake sets all of that up in a moment, and automated authorities such as Let's Encrypt have made certificates something most sites can get without cost or manual effort. The remaining risks usually come from details around the edges, such as insecure subresources and unprotected first requests, which is why redirects, HSTS, and clean page assets are worth the attention.

Sources

[1] MDN Web Docs, Transport Layer Security (TLS) - https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Transport_Layer_Security
[2] Let's Encrypt, How It Works - https://letsencrypt.org/how-it-works/

title: How Heat Pumps Work and Why They Cut Home Heating Energy
summary: How heat pumps work, why they use less energy than gas boilers, how they perform in cold climates, and what sizing and incentives to check before buying.
seo: how heat pumps work, heat pump efficiency, air source heat pump, cold climate heat pump, home heating emissions
author: knowledge blog
content:
Heating a building is one of the largest uses of energy worldwide, and it is also one of the more stubborn sources of emissions. Heat pumps are often described as a way to reduce both energy use and carbon dioxide from heating. But how can a machine that runs on electricity deliver more heat than the electricity it consumes, and does it really work when the weather is freezing? This article explains the basic idea, summarizes what the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the U.S. ENERGY STAR program say, and lists practical points to check before considering one. It is general information, not advice for a particular home.

The core idea: moving heat instead of making it

A gas boiler or electric resistance heater creates heat by burning fuel or by passing current through an element. A heat pump moves heat that already exists. In winter it collects heat from outside air, the ground, or water, even when it feels cold, and delivers it indoors. Many models can also run in reverse in summer, taking heat out of the building the way an air conditioner does.

The moving is done with a refrigerant, a fluid that changes between liquid and gas. A compressor squeezes the gas, which raises its temperature, and the hot gas gives up heat to the indoor air or water as it condenses back into a liquid. An expansion valve then lowers the pressure, the fluid evaporates outdoors, absorbing heat from the surroundings, and the cycle repeats. This is the same cycle found in a refrigerator, applied in the opposite direction for heating. Describing the refrigerant cycle is standard physics background rather than a claim taken from the two sources cited below.

Because electricity is used to run the compressor and fans rather than to create the heat directly, the delivered heat can exceed the electrical input. The IEA reports that heat pumps currently available on the market are three to five times more energy efficient than natural gas boilers [1]. The comparison is between energy efficiency in typical operation, so real results depend on climate, installation, and how the system is used.

Why heating matters for energy and climate

The IEA's scale of the issue is striking. It says that over one sixth of global natural gas demand is used for heating buildings, and in the European Union that share is one third. Heating in buildings is responsible for 4 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions each year, which is 10 percent of global emissions [1]. These figures come from a 2022 report, so they describe the situation at that time rather than today.

The agency concludes that heat pumps powered by low-emissions electricity are the central technology for a secure and sustainable heating transition. It adds that installing heat pumps in place of fossil-fuel boilers significantly reduces greenhouse gas emissions in all major heating markets, even with the current electricity mix, and that the advantage grows as electricity grids decarbonize [1]. In other words, a heat pump does not need a perfectly clean grid to come out ahead, though a cleaner grid improves the result.

Are heat pumps ready for cold weather?

A common worry is that heat pumps only suit mild climates. The IEA offers evidence against the blanket version of that claim: it says that in Norway, 60 percent of buildings were equipped with heat pumps, with Sweden and Finland above 40 percent, which undercuts the argument that heat pumps are unsuitable for cold climates [1].

ENERGY STAR, the U.S. government-backed efficiency program, explains the technology behind this. Many new certified air source heat pumps provide space heating even in the coldest climates, because they use advanced compressors and refrigerants that improve low-temperature performance. ENERGY STAR's cold climate certification requires third-party verified performance testing down to 5 degrees Fahrenheit. The program adds that a cold climate unit will keep working below 5 degrees Fahrenheit, but pairing it with a back-up energy source heats a home most efficiently when temperatures fall even lower [2]. Note the nuance: modern units can handle cold, but the program itself recommends talking with a contractor about the right unit and whether to include a back-up system.

Sizing and installation matter

A heat pump that is too large or too small for the home will struggle. ENERGY STAR says that proper sizing is essential for the best performance and comfort, and that a contractor should verify the right size with a calculation called Manual J, which estimates how much heating and cooling a home requires [2]. This ties to a point the IEA makes about buildings themselves. Households that add a heat pump without improving efficiency in parallel can nearly triple their peak winter electricity demand. Improving a home's efficiency rating by two grades, for example from D to B in European countries, can halve heating energy demand and reduce the heat pump size needed [1]. Practical translation: insulation and air sealing do not compete with a heat pump, they make a smaller and cheaper system possible.

Dual fuel systems

ENERGY STAR describes a dual fuel option for homes that already have a relatively new furnace paired with an older central air conditioner. Adding a certified heat pump creates a system that can heat with either the heat pump or the traditional furnace, allowing each to be used according to cost and environmental benefit [2]. For some households this can be a stepping stone, keeping the existing furnace as a backup while shifting most heating to electricity.

Costs, savings, and incentives

The IEA says that, over their lifetime, heat pumps can save consumers money and protect them from fuel price shocks. It reports that the average household or business using a heat pump spends less on energy than one using a gas boiler, and that these savings offset the higher upfront cost in many markets, in some even without subsidies. Its estimates of household savings, made in the context of the 2022 energy price spike, ranged from 300 US dollars per year in the United States to 900 US dollars in Europe [1]. Prices change, so check current local energy rates before assuming those figures apply to you.

ENERGY STAR notes that although these products can cost more upfront, the difference is repaid over time through lower energy bills. It also says certified air source heat pumps are eligible for a federal tax credit of up to 2,000 US dollars for products purchased and installed between January 1, 2023 and December 31, 2032, and that many utilities offer incentives as well [2]. Incentive rules can change over time and vary by location, so confirm the current terms with ENERGY STAR or your utility before relying on them.

Grid impacts and bigger picture

Widespread heat pump use means more electricity demand. The IEA reports that in a scenario where governments meet their announced climate and energy commitments, the share of electricity in building and industry heating doubles between 2021 and 2030 to 16 percent. Over the same period global electricity demand rises by a quarter, and heat pumps contribute less than one tenth of that rise. The agency says that efficiency improvements, demand response, and careful grid planning can greatly reduce the strain [1]. Heat pumps are also not limited to homes. The IEA notes that large heat pumps can provide heat up to 140 to 160 degrees Celsius for industry, with the paper, food, and chemicals sectors having the largest near-term opportunities [1].

Questions to ask before buying

What size does a Manual J calculation recommend for this home? [2] Is a cold climate certified model appropriate where I live, and do I need a back-up heat source? [2] Can I improve insulation or air sealing first, or at the same time? [1] What incentives and utility rebates apply now? [2] How does my local electricity price compare with my current fuel price? [1]

Takeaway

Heat pumps work by moving heat, which is why they can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity. The IEA's analysis supports their role in cutting heating emissions and energy bills, and ENERGY STAR's guidance shows that cold weather is a design question rather than an automatic barrier. The outcome in any single building depends on sizing, insulation, local prices, and the electricity mix, so treat the headline numbers as a starting point and get a qualified contractor's assessment.

Sources

[1] International Energy Agency, The Future of Heat Pumps: Executive Summary - https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-heat-pumps/executive-summary
[2] ENERGY STAR, Air Source Heat Pumps - https://www.energystar.gov/products/air_source_heat_pumps
